                programming environment, or
                @243 <code> lua
                the programming language of that environment. I still don’t know them well today, but have acquired some intuition of their capabilities and mechanisms. Here I would like to talk about the stack I cr…
                @246 <a aria-label="Link to paragraph" class=anchor-link href=#p-1> #
              @249 <p id=p-2>

                        a sneak peek of

              @296 <hr>
              @298 <p id=p-3>
                In this first post, I’d like to take a historical view on how this “AI-native” development stack was built conservatively from the ground up (reverse of
                @300 <a href=https://steve-yegge.medium.com/welcome-to-gas-town-4f25ee16dd04> Gas Town
                ), and came into its current shape. The key philosophy I follow in its design:
                @303 <a aria-label="Link to paragraph" class=anchor-link href=#p-3> #
              @306 <ol>
                @308 <li> Keep all state in a single repository, in text format. This allows AI to access not only code, but design documents, issue history, past roadmaps etc., everything, using the standard set of Unix tool…
                @311 <li> Construct a “hard deterministic shell” to constrain an LLM’s “soft stochastic core”. Ground often.
                @314 <li> Human attention is scarce and single-threaded and it is diametrically opposed to what machines are good at. This AI-native stack tries to find that evolving contour of where, when, and how to leverag…
              @318 <p id=p-4>
                We will talk more about this in the next post.
                @320 <a aria-label="Link to paragraph" class=anchor-link href=#p-4> #
              @323 <hr>
              @325 <p id=p-5>
                Now, quick history recap. I took the anti-
                @327 <code> Gas Town
                approach and started very conservatively. I needed to know how building blocks work, and how well they work, before moving to construct more things on top of those building blocks. What’s extremely r…
                @330 <a href=/2026/10/5-month-coding-stats> overall journey
                produced about
                @333 <strong> 1M
                lines of code,
                @336 <strong> 1M
                lines of supporting documentation (issues, plans, reviews etc.).
                @339 <a aria-label="Link to paragraph" class=anchor-link href=#p-5> #
              @342 <ol>
                @344 <li>
                  @346 <p id=p-6>
                    At the start, I was basically using the plain old coding agent.
                    @348 <code> Claude Code
                    ,
                    @351 <code> Codex
                    are the main players, but there are plenty of other companies also trying (I used
                    @354 <code> agy
                    ,
                    @357 <code> muse
                    ,
                    @360 <code> qoder
                    ). You type a prompt, and hope for the best, frequently back and forth in a really crappy editor. Those were the early days of my vibe coding, but AI showed great potential. I didn’t use too many age…
                    @363 <code> superpowers
                    . The reason being, if I don’t know how those skills work, and how well they work, I can’t trust them. Thus it seemed logical to limit how many of those I’d use. You can check my early notes
                    @366 <a href=/2025/05/ai-coding-take-2> here
                    and
                    @369 <a href=/2025/04/reflection-on-ai-coding> here
                    .
                    @372 <a aria-label="Link to paragraph" class=anchor-link href=#p-6> #
                @376 <li>
                  @378 <p id=p-7>
                    One of the early choices I made was that all state should be in a single repository, the issues, the plans, the projects, the roadmaps. All those should be text files in a repository so that changing…
                    @380 <a aria-label="Link to paragraph" class=anchor-link href=#p-7> #
                @384 <li>
                  @386 <p id=p-8>
                    And then, to manage those local text files, I used AI to make tools for me, e.g. a neovim plugin to list all open issue files, to open one of them nicely formatted, and to jump to interlinked issue I…
                    @388 <a aria-label="Link to paragraph" class=anchor-link href=#p-8> #
                  @391 <p>
                    @392 <img alt="The issue tracker in Neovim, listing open and in-progress issues" src=/assets/images/2026-10-03-issue-tracker.png>
                  @394 <p>
                    @395 <img alt="One issue opened from the tracker, showing its front matter: status, dates, est…" src=/assets/images/2026-10-03-issue-detail.png>
                @398 <li>
                  @400 <p id=p-9>
                    Soon, I realized it’s painful to use
                    @402 <code> claude
                    or
                    @405 <code> codex
                    really, the tiny input box, without mouse support, or any other editor goodies. I wanted something closer to a text editor, than a command line prompt. This led me to create
                    @408 <a href=https://github.com/xianxu/pair> pair
                    , which is a TTY terminal wrapper around any TUI program, but coding agents in particular, and gives you an input pane backed by nvim. With that, you get mouse support, all nvim goodies, spell checki…
                    @411 <code> pair
                    as a coding agent wrapper that gives you much more control over how you organize your thought. Another fundamental benefit is to allow you to use any coding agent without changing the user interface …
                    @414 <code> claude
                    outages surely motivated me to actually commit to it.
                    @417 <a aria-label="Link to paragraph" class=anchor-link href=#p-9> #
                  @420 <p>
                    @421 <img alt="pair: Claude Code on top, with the nvim input pane below it" src=/assets/images/2026-10-03-pair-review.png>
                @424 <li>
                  @426 <p id=p-10>
                    With the process documents (issues, projects, roadmaps etc. whatever you need to run a company’s product/engineering department) managed in the same repository, the other part is to get the agent to …
                    @428 <a href=/2026/06/skill-binary-and-dynamic-skill> skill binaries
                    ”, which operates around two intuitions: 1/ to move as many operations as possible to deterministic code; 2/ that deterministic code can also administer the skill prose. The result’s refreshing: the
                    @431 <code> sdlc
                    process (software development life cycle) is just a Golang binary, with
                    @434 <code> sdlc --help
                    being what the agent needs to read and understand. This basically converts an agent skill into just another local tool, just another
                    @437 <code> grep
                    ,
                    @440 <code> rg
                    etc. Other extensions involve the ability to dynamically customize skill content based on repository state, for example, I used it to construct a meta skill to instruct the agent on how to use the ev…
                    @443 <code> datatype
                    defined in different
                    @446 <code> ariadne
                    base layers (see point 6).
                    @449 <a aria-label="Link to paragraph" class=anchor-link href=#p-10> #
                @453 <li>
                  @455 <p id=p-11>
                    I called my AI-native workflow
                    @457 <a href=https://github.com/xianxu/ariadne> ariadne
                    , which is a provider of
                    @460 <code> base layers
                    .
                    @463 <code> ariadne
                    , the base layer, provides basic process around software development. There are other base layers, for example, I have a
                    @466 <code> nous
                    base layer that is layered on top of
                    @469 <code> ariadne
                    as a personal gateway to private information, imagine a repository full of your gmail downloaded, but with credentials guarded by the “hard shell”;
                    @472 <code> metis
                    which provides essentially what typical ML infra is about, organizing data, algorithms, experiments, to provide a reproducible workflow. Base layers like
                    @475 <code> ariadne
                    ,
                    @478 <code> metis
                    ,
                    @481 <code> nous
                    are meant to be used as follows: you start with your repository, and if you want to leverage AI’s capability in a base layer, you invoke
                    @484 <code> weave link ../ariadne
                    , or
                    @487 <code> weave link ../metis
                    in the repository root, then
                    @490 <code> weave compile
                    from there. That’s all you need. What do those two commands provide you? Two things: 1/ agent skills to manage some processes; 2/ a binary “hard shell” that makes those processes work. I created
                    @493 <code> metis
                    and
                    @496 <code> nous
                    not quite for fun, but as validation of this construct of base layers, in very different domains. For example, I got a Kaggle silver medal with
                    @499 <code> metis
                    in some oil drilling competition that I didn’t have any experience in.
                    @502 <a aria-label="Link to paragraph" class=anchor-link href=#p-11> #
                @506 <li>
                  @508 <p id=p-12>
                    After I created
                    @510 <code> pair
                    , the TTY wrapper, I used to use iTerm2, then Ghostty, and later cmux. None of them were satisfactory, because those environments don’t provide support of working on many threads at the same time. I …
                    @513 <code> couch
                    , a single program that supervises many
                    @516 <code> pair
                    programs. One way to think of
                    @519 <code> couch
                    is just the many tabs and panes in your favorite terminal emulators.
                    @522 <code> couch
                    does that, and provides many shortcuts you need in an agentic environment, that get your human attention at the right place at the right time, such as managing the different worktrees for you, showin…
                    @525 <code> couch
                    also provides a protocol through which different coding agents can talk to each other, so that you can work with
                    @528 <code> claude
                    in a slot triaging issues in a repository, and then just say “schedule it”, and
                    @531 <code> couch
                    will find a free slot (worktree), talk with the agent there, so that the free agent starts handling the task. After the agent’s done, it will send a smoke-test notification if needed, so the operator…
                    @534 <code> couch
                    is pretty usable now; the autonomous agent coordinator aspect is still being tested out.
                    @537 <a aria-label="Link to paragraph" class=anchor-link href=#p-12> #
                  @540 <p>
                    @541 <img alt="couch: a pair session beside a terminal, with the bar of repositories and slots…" src=/assets/images/2026-10-03-couch.png>
